summary: Presents service provider requirements for MPLS traffic engineering that is aware of Differentiated Services. It aims to guide the definition and selection of a technical solution but does not specify one. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3564 lists what providers need from MPLS traffic engineering that treats different service classes separately. It sets requirements for a future design but does not define the design itself.

questions: what is a class-type in mpls
subtitle: Requirements for steering each class of MPLS traffic under its own bandwidth limits.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering applies one bandwidth limit across all traffic classes. Providers may need separate limits to control how much of each class uses a link.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes provider scenarios and requirements for Diff-Serv-aware traffic engineering, including Class-Types, bandwidth-constraint models, and preemption behavior.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements and ways to evaluate a future solution, but does not specify that solution. RFC 3564 was updated by RFC 5462.

facts.label: TE-Classes
facts.value: Up to 8 supported from 64 possible combinations

today: RFC 3564 is an Informational document that was updated by RFC 5462. It sets requirements for DS-TE but does not specify a technical solution.

sections.title: Why Traffic Classes Need Separate Limits
sections.content:
Providers use Differentiated Services (Diff-Serv) to give packets different treatment. Existing MPLS traffic engineering can optimize paths, but applies one shared bandwidth constraint across all Diff-Serv classes.

Diff-Serv-aware traffic engineering (DS-TE) assigns traffic from different classes to separate Label Switched Paths (LSPs). It can then select paths and enforce bandwidth limits based on each class's needs. The memo addresses operation within one administrative domain, not between domains.
sections.plainLanguage: DS-TE lets a network manage paths for each service class separately. This matters when one shared bandwidth limit cannot protect each class's needs.

sections.title: Provider Scenarios
sections.content:
The memo gives three reasons providers may need separate constraints. They may want to limit the share of a link used by delay-sensitive traffic, keep class proportions aligned with scheduler settings after failures, or reserve a bounded share for traffic sold with guaranteed bandwidth.

In each case, a single aggregate limit cannot express the desired policy for all classes. DS-TE must allow different bandwidth constraints to govern different groups of traffic trunks.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider may need to cap one class, preserve planned shares after a failure, or protect guaranteed service. Separate limits let the network express those policies.

sections.title: Class-Types and Bandwidth Constraints
sections.content:
A Class-Type (CT) is a set of traffic trunks on a link governed by a particular set of bandwidth constraints. A traffic trunk belongs to the same CT on every link. The solution MUST support up to 8 CTs and at least 2, while allowing operators to deploy fewer than the maximum.

A bandwidth-constraint model specifies how many constraints exist and which CTs each one governs. The RFC illustrates a Maximum Allocation Model, with a separate limit per CT, and a Russian Doll model, with nested limits covering groups of CTs. A solution MUST support multiple models and up to 8 constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: A Class-Type groups traffic that follows the same bandwidth rules. The design must support several groups without forcing a network to use every available group.

sections.title: Preemption and TE-Classes
sections.content:
DS-TE must retain existing preemption behavior across Class-Types. An LSP with a higher setup priority may preempt another LSP when they compete for a resource, subject to the existing setup and holding priority rules. An operator must also be able to disable preemption.

A TE-Class pairs a Class-Type with a preemption priority. There are 8 priorities and up to 8 Class-Types, so 64 combinations are possible. The practical requirement is support for up to 8 TE-Classes, chosen from those combinations.
sections.plainLanguage: A TE-Class pairs a traffic group with a priority. The rules preserve the existing way higher-priority paths can take resources from eligible lower-priority paths.

sections.title: Evaluating a Solution and Security
sections.content:
The memo does not select a protocol design. It says candidate solutions may extend existing traffic-engineering protocol syntax or change how existing fields are interpreted. Evaluation must consider whether a solution meets the scenarios, its flexibility, extensibility, scalability, backward compatibility, migration, and bandwidth-constraint models.

A DS-TE solution must address security. It must not weaken existing MPLS traffic-engineering or Diff-Serv protections, including protections against denial-of-service attacks; otherwise, it must provide safeguards to address the gap.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives criteria for comparing future designs, but leaves the choice open. Any design must preserve existing security protections or replace them with adequate safeguards.
